"How much is my case worth?" is the first question nearly every injured person asks, and it is a perfectly reasonable one. You are dealing with medical bills, lost wages, and pain that was not your fault. You want a number. Unfortunately, the internet is full of vague statistics that create false expectations, and insurance companies use those same numbers to lowball you. This guide breaks down realistic settlement ranges by case type, explains the factors that actually move the needle, and covers how Georgia and South Carolina law shapes what you can recover.

According to the Bureau of Justice Statistics, the median personal injury award in state courts is roughly $31,000, but that single number is almost meaningless. The gap between a minor fender-bender and a catastrophic brain injury is enormous, and your case will land somewhere on that spectrum based on facts that are unique to you.

Unfortunately, the internet is full of vague statistics that create false expectations, and insurance companies use those same numbers to lowball you. before: The word "average" suggests a reliable middle ground, but personal injury settlements do not follow a neat bell curve. A handful of multimillion-dollar verdicts in wrongful death and catastrophic injury cases pull the mean far above what most people receive. Meanwhile, thousands of soft-tissue claims settle for $5,000 to $15,000 and drag the median down. Neither number tells you what your case is worth.

Settlement Ranges by Case Type

The table below provides general ranges based on the type of accident and the severity of injuries involved. These are not guarantees. They reflect the broad spectrum of outcomes our attorneys see in Georgia and South Carolina personal injury claims.

Case Type Typical Settlement Range Key Variables
Car Accident $15,000 – $75,000 Injury severity, fault percentage, policy limits
Truck Accident $50,000 – $500,000+ Federal regulation violations, multiple liable parties, catastrophic injuries
Motorcycle Accident $30,000 – $150,000 Road rash severity, helmet use, bias against riders
Slip and Fall $10,000 – $50,000 Property owner notice, hazard documentation, pre-existing conditions
Medical Malpractice $100,000 – $1,000,000+ Standard of care deviation, expert testimony costs, damage permanence
Wrongful Death $500,000 – $5,000,000+ Decedent's earning capacity, number of dependents, egregiousness of conduct
Brain Injury $100,000 – $10,000,000+ Cognitive impairment level, lifetime care costs, lost earning capacity
Dog Bite $15,000 – $50,000 Scarring and disfigurement, infection complications, owner's prior knowledge

The wide ranges exist for a reason. A car accident that results in whiplash and six weeks of physical therapy is a fundamentally different case than one that results in a spinal cord injury requiring surgery and months of rehabilitation. Both are car accidents, but their settlement values are worlds apart.
after:
What the Data Shows by Case Type

No reliable source publishes settlement ranges by case type. The closest published figures below are not settlement averages: they are median trial awards to plaintiffs who won (Bureau of Justice Statistics, 2005 data) and, for car accidents, the 2024 average auto bodily-injury liability claim payment, including loss-adjustment expenses (Insurance Information Institute, citing ISO). Settlements vary widely.

Case Type Published Figure (Not a Settlement Average) Key Variables
Car Accident $15,000 median trial award (BJS, 2005); $28,278 average bodily-injury liability claim payment (III/ISO, 2024) Injury severity, fault percentage, policy limits
Truck Accident No reliable published figure Federal regulation violations, multiple liable parties, catastrophic injuries
Motorcycle Accident No reliable published figure Road rash severity, helmet use, bias against riders
Slip and Fall $98,000 median premises-liability trial award (BJS, 2005) Property owner notice, hazard documentation, pre-existing conditions
Medical Malpractice $400,000 median trial award (BJS, 2005) Standard of care deviation, expert testimony costs, damage permanence
Wrongful Death No reliable published figure Decedent's earning capacity, number of dependents, egregiousness of conduct
Brain Injury No reliable published figure Cognitive impairment level, lifetime care costs, lost earning capacity
Dog Bite $21,000 median animal-attack trial award (BJS, 2005) Scarring and disfigurement, infection complications, owner's prior knowledge

Even within one case type, outcomes vary widely. A car accident that results in whiplash and six weeks of physical therapy is a fundamentally different case than one that results in a spinal cord injury requiring surgery and months of rehabilitation. Both are car accidents, but their settlement values are worlds apart.

before:
No cap on compensatory damages. Georgia does not impose a statutory cap on compensatory damages in most personal injury cases, including pain and suffering. Medical malpractice damage caps were struck down by the Georgia Supreme Court in Atlanta Oculoplastic Surgery, P.C. v. Nestlehutt (2010), so there is no artificial ceiling on what a jury can award.

Punitive damages. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1), with exceptions for cases involving product liability, specific intent to harm, or conduct under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
after:
No cap on compensatory damages. Georgia does not impose a statutory cap on compensatory damages in most personal injury cases, including pain and suffering. Georgia's caps on noneconomic damages in medical malpractice cases were struck down by the Georgia Supreme Court in Atlanta Oculoplastic Surgery, P.C. v. Nestlehutt (2010), so there is no artificial ceiling on what a jury can award.

2025 tort reform (SB 68). Since April 21, 2025, lawyers may suggest a dollar figure for pain and suffering only in closing argument, and only if it is rationally related to the evidence, even in pending cases (O.C.G.A. § 9-10-184). For injuries on or after that date, medical expenses are limited to the reasonable value of necessary care, and if you have health insurance the jury may hear what your insurer actually paid as well as the billed amount (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-1.1). Seat-belt non-use is now admissible evidence (O.C.G.A. § 40-8-76.1).

Punitive damages. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1), with exceptions for cases involving product liability, specific intent to harm, or conduct under the influence of drugs or alcohol to the point that judgment was substantially impaired.

before:
No cap on actual damages. South Carolina does not cap compensatory damages, including non-economic damages like pain and suffering, in standard personal injury cases. This means that a jury can award whatever amount it finds appropriate based on the evidence.

Punitive damages. South Carolina caps punitive damages at the greater of three times the compensatory damages or $739,245, the 2026 inflation-indexed figure (S.C. Code § 15-32-530). This cap does not apply in cases involving drunk driving or intentional conduct.
after:
Limited caps on actual damages. South Carolina does not cap compensatory damages, including non-economic damages like pain and suffering, in standard personal injury cases. This means that a jury can award whatever amount it finds appropriate based on the evidence. The exceptions are medical malpractice, where noneconomic damages are capped (inflation-adjusted to $596,001 per defendant and $1,788,002 total in 2026, S.C. Code § 15-32-220), and claims against government entities, capped at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence (S.C. Code § 15-78-120).

Punitive damages. South Carolina caps punitive damages at the greater of three times the compensatory damages or $739,245, the 2026 inflation-indexed figure (S.C. Code § 15-32-530). The cap does not apply when the defendant was impaired by alcohol or drugs, intended to cause harm, or pleaded guilty to or was convicted of a felony for the same conduct, and it rises to the greater of four times compensatory damages or $2 million for certain profit-motivated misconduct or conduct that could support a felony conviction.

before: A settlement is a negotiated agreement between you and the insurance company or defendant. You agree to accept a specific amount of money in exchange for releasing your legal claims. Settlements happen before trial, sometimes before a lawsuit is even filed. The vast majority of personal injury cases, roughly 95% or more, resolve through settlement.
after: A settlement is a negotiated agreement between you and the insurance company or defendant. You agree to accept a specific amount of money in exchange for releasing your legal claims. Settlements happen before trial, sometimes before a lawsuit is even filed. The vast majority of personal injury cases resolve without a trial: in the most recent Bureau of Justice Statistics count (2005), only about 4% of tort cases in state courts were decided by a judge or jury, and most of the rest settled.

before: Going to trial carries risk. It also takes longer and costs more due to expert witness fees, court costs, and the additional attorney time involved. However, the willingness to go to trial is one of the most powerful tools in settlement negotiations. Insurance companies track which attorneys actually try cases and which ones always settle. Firms that go to trial when necessary tend to get better settlement offers because the insurance company knows the threat is real.
after: Going to trial carries risk. It also takes longer and costs more due to expert witness fees, court costs, and the additional attorney time involved. However, the willingness to go to trial is one of the most powerful tools in settlement negotiations. Insurers weigh the realistic risk that a case will go to a jury, and that risk is more credible when your attorney is prepared to try it.

before: National averages are misleading. Ranges by type: car accidents $15K-$75K, truck $50K-$500K+, slip and fall $10K-$50K, med mal $100K-$1M+, wrongful death $500K-$5M+.
after: There is no reliable national average for settlements, because insurers do not publish them and every case turns on its own injuries, evidence and insurance. The closest federal data are trial verdicts: in the Bureau of Justice Statistics' most recent study (2005 data), half of plaintiffs who won a tort trial in state court were awarded $24,000 or less, with a median of $15,000 in car-accident trials and $400,000 in medical-malpractice trials. An attorney who reviews your records can give you a realistic range.

before: About 95% settle before trial. Having an attorney prepared to go to trial leads to higher settlement offers.
after: Most settle. In the most recent Bureau of Justice Statistics count (2005 data), only about 4% of tort cases in state courts ended in a trial. An attorney who is prepared to try your case gives the insurer a real reason to make a fair offer.

before: Most settle 6-18 months after MMI. Complex cases can take 2-3 years.
after: It depends on your treatment and the insurer. Most claims are not ready to settle until your treatment reaches maximum medical improvement, and cases that go into litigation take longer.
